title: this, const Member Functions and Chaining
summary: Inside a member function, `this` points at the object the function was called on. Mark every function that does not modify the object `const`: only those can be called on `const` objects. Return `*this` by reference to allow **chaining**.
ideas:
1. Build a `StringBuilder` with chainable `append`, `appendLine` and `repeat`, and a `const` function `str`.
2. Make a `const` object of one of your classes and call every member function on it. Add the missing `const`s.
3. Give a class both a const and a non-const `at` and check which one each call uses.

cards.q: What is the type of `this` in a non-const member function of `T`?
cards.a:
`T*`

`this` is a pointer to the object. In a `const` member function it is `const T*`.

So further calls can be chained on the same object without copying it

Returning `T&` to `*this` lets you write `obj.setA(1).setB(2)`, with each call acting on the same object.

cards.q: Why should a function that changes nothing still be marked `const`?
cards.a:
Without it, it cannot be called on a const object or `const&`

A const object only allows const member functions. Leaving `const` off makes perfectly safe getters unusable through a `const&`.

A member to be modified inside a `const` member function

`mutable` is for members that do not affect the object's visible value, such as a cache or a mutex.
